AI research doesn't happen in silos — the most impactful work sits at the intersections. This page maps how agents, reasoning, retrieval, and multi-modal systems relate to each other. ```{mermaid} flowchart TB subgraph Core["Core AI Capabilities"] R[LLM Reasoning
Chain-of-thought, planning, verification] RET[RAG & Retrieval
Dense search, knowledge graphs, citations] MM[Multi-Modal Models
Vision, audio, document understanding] end subgraph Agent["AI Agents"] A[Autonomous Agents
Tool use, multi-step planning, memory] end R --> A RET --> A MM --> A A -->|agents reason about
what to retrieve| RET A -->|agents use reasoning
to plan actions| R A -->|agents perceive via
multi-modal inputs| MM R <-->|reasoning grounded
in retrieved facts| RET R <-->|reasoning over images,
audio, documents| MM RET <-->|retrieval enhanced
by visual/semantic cues| MM style Agent fill:#2d5016,stroke:#4a7c28,color:#fff style Core fill:#1a3a5c,stroke:#2d5f8a,color:#fff ``` ## Key Intersections ### Agents + Reasoning Agents need reasoning to decide what to do next. The ReAct paradigm interleaves thinking and acting: the agent reasons about which tool to call, observes the result, then reasons again. Recent work on **efficiency-aware reasoning** (early exit, token budgets) directly impacts agent cost — an agent that over-thinks each step becomes prohibitively expensive. **Key papers:** [SABER](topics/llm-reasoning.html) (early exit for reasoning), [Thinking Costs Tokens](topics/llm-reasoning.html) (token budget thresholds) ### Agents + Retrieval Agents use retrieval to access knowledge they don't have in parameters. **Agentic RAG** flips the traditional pipeline: instead of always retrieving, the agent decides *when* to retrieve, *what* to retrieve, and *how* to use results. This is more flexible than fixed retrieve-then-generate pipelines. **Key papers:** [CareGraph](topics/ai-agents.html) (knowledge graphs for agents), [Cross-Session Decomposition Attacks](topics/rag-retrieval.html) (safety of retrieval in agents) ### Agents + Multi-Modal Modern agents operate in visual environments. **GUI agents** (like WM-R1) perceive screens, reason about UI elements, and take actions like clicking or typing. **Multimodal search agents** (like WeAgent-MMSearch) keep retrieved images in context for visually grounded reasoning. **Key papers:** [WM-R1](topics/ai-agents.html) (world models for GUI agents), [WeAgent-MMSearch](topics/multi-modal.html) (text-vision interaction) ### Reasoning + Retrieval Reasoning benefits enormously from retrieval. When a model retrieves relevant facts before reasoning, it reduces hallucination and improves factual accuracy. Conversely, reasoning can improve retrieval — a model can decompose a complex query into sub-queries, or verify retrieved facts through logical consistency. **Key papers:** [RRDF](topics/rag-retrieval.html) (RAG for fallacy detection), [Financial Numerical Reasoning](topics/llm-reasoning.html) (retrieval-grounded reasoning) ### Reasoning + Multi-Modal Multi-modal inputs create new reasoning challenges. A model must reason about visual relationships, spatial layouts, and temporal sequences — not just text. **Document understanding** combines OCR, layout analysis, and semantic reasoning. **Visual question answering** requires grounding text reasoning in visual evidence. **Key papers:** [See, Hypothesize, Validate](topics/multi-modal.html) (multimodal PDE discovery), [Nemotron 3.5](topics/multi-modal.html) (multimodal safety reasoning) ### Retrieval + Multi-Modal Retrieval isn't just for text. **Image retrieval** finds visually similar images using learned embedding" onclick="window.location.href='wiki.html'">embedding" onclick="window.location.href='wiki.html'">embeddings. **Document retrieval** handles PDFs, slides, and scanned pages. **Cross-modal retrieval** maps queries in one modality to documents in another (e.g., text query → image results). **Key papers:** [MAP Benchmark](topics/multi-modal.html) (accessibility-aware place retrieval), [CoRe-MoE](topics/multi-modal.html) (continual learning for retrieval tasks) ## Learning Paths Depending on your background, here are suggested reading orders: ### Path 1: New to AI → Agents 1. Start with [LLM Reasoning foundations](topics/llm-reasoning.html#foundations) — understand how models think 2. Read [RAG foundations](topics/rag-retrieval.html#foundations) — understand how models access knowledge 3. Read [Multi-Modal foundations](topics/multi-modal.html#foundations) — understand how models perceive 4. Finally, [AI Agents](topics/ai-agents.html) — see how it all comes together ### Path 2: Software Engineer → Agents 1. Start with [AI Agents foundations](topics/ai-agents.html#foundations) — the architecture you'll build 2. Read [RAG foundations](topics/rag-retrieval.html#foundations) — how to give agents knowledge 3. Browse the [Glossary](glossary.html) for tool-use and planning terms 4. Dive into [agent papers](topics/ai-agents.html#recent-papers) for state of the art ### Path 3: ML Researcher → Cutting Edge 1. Read the [latest digest](digests/week-2026-35.html) for this week's developments 2. Browse [papers by date](papers/index.html) for the newest work 3. Use the [Glossary](glossary.html) to quickly look up unfamiliar terms 4. Follow cross-links between topics to trace research threads
